headline: AI slop is flooding your feed, and it pays

sources.title: What is AI slop? Why you are seeing more fake photos and videos in your feeds (The Conversation)
AI slop's meteoric rise and the impact of synthetic content in 2026 (Digital Watch Observatory)
AI Slop won in 2025 - fingerprinting real content might be the answer in 2026 (TechRadar)
AI Slop Is Destroying The Internet (video, Kurzgesagt)

chunks.text: A bear doing a [[backflip]] on a trampoline. A baby made of spaghetti. A famous actor celebrating his 1800th birthday. None of it is real, but it is everywhere. [[Critics]] call it [[AI slop]]: cheap, strange [[content]] created by [[artificial intelligence]] in seconds. New AI tools can {{pump out}} this [[material]] faster than any human could type, and the fake posts now {{clog up}} feeds on every major app.

verbs.correct: To produce quickly in large amounts
verbs.why: A factory can pump out a thousand toys an hour, and a busy kitchen can pump out fresh bread all morning. New AI tools now pump out fake photos and videos faster than any person could type.

verbs.correct: To block something so it cannot flow
verbs.why: Fallen leaves clog up a drain after a storm, and holiday traffic clogs up the highway every year. Now these fake posts clog up feeds on every major app, leaving little room for anything real.

chunks.text: Why does the internet [[drown]] in slop? Because it pays. Millions of people {{fall for}} the fake photos and share them, and every click means [[advertising]] money. Big [[platforms]] reward popular posts with real payments, so slop [[factories]] treat fake content like a business: it costs almost nothing to make, and one viral [[hit]] can {{rake in}} more than a month of honest work. One writer described slop as [[clickbait]] with a brain. The [[algorithm]] cannot tell the difference, and often it does not care.

verbs.correct: To believe a trick is real
verbs.wrong: To pay too much for something
verbs.why: Grandparents sometimes fall for a phone scam, and shoppers fall for an ad that promises free money. Millions of people fall for these fake AI photos and share them without a second thought.

verbs.correct: To earn a lot of money quickly
verbs.why: A hit movie can rake in millions in one weekend, and an ice cream shop can rake in cash during a heat wave. Here one viral fake post can rake in more money than a month of honest work.

chunks.text: The good news: most slop still makes mistakes, and those mistakes {{give away}} the fakes. Look closely and you may find hands with six fingers, [[shadows]] pointing in different directions, or [[background]] details that simply do not {{add up}}. Experts say readers should {{look out for}} strange hands, [[melted]] letters, and too-perfect faces, and always check the original [[sources]] before believing a photo.

verbs.correct: To show the hidden truth about something
verbs.why: Shaking hands can give away a person's nerves, and a small smile can give away a hidden secret. Here strange shadows and extra fingers give away a photo that was never real.

verbs.correct: To make sense as a whole
verbs.wrong: To happen at the same time
verbs.why: A messy story about a broken window does not always add up, and a set of receipts should always add up at the end. In a fake photo, background details often do not add up, and that is how careful readers spot them.

verbs.wrong: To fix something before it breaks
verbs.why: Drivers look out for deer at night, and shoppers look out for fake price tags on sale days. Experts want readers to look out for strange hands, melted letters, and faces that look too perfect.

chunks.text: Some [[accounts]] posting slop have millions of followers, and companies promise to {{crack down on}} the worst [[offenders]]. But as long as fake [[views]] earn real money, the [[flood]] will not {{die down}} soon. Until then, the best defense costs nothing: when a video looks too strange to be true, just {{scroll past}} without a second look. Every [[ignored]] fake makes slop a little less [[profitable]].

verbs.why: Police crack down on speeding drivers near schools, and cities crack down on illegal parking downtown. Big platforms now promise to crack down on the accounts that post the worst fake content.
Strong wind usually dies down by morning, and loud laughter dies down once the joke gets old. As long as fake views earn real money, this flood of AI content will not die down soon.

verbs.correct: To skip something on a screen
verbs.why: Use scroll past for a quick habit on a phone, moving through post after post without stopping to look closely. The simplest defense against a fake video is to scroll past it, since every ignored fake earns less money for its maker.

mainIdea.s: Cheap AI-made photos and videos are flooding social media because they earn advertising money. Experts explain how to spot the fakes and why the problem will continue.
mainIdea.why: Slop is almost free to make, platforms reward popular posts, and mistakes like strange hands still give away the fakes.

mainIdea.s: AI companies are paying social apps to fill feeds with test videos so their tools can learn. The strange clips will disappear once the training finishes later this year.
mainIdea.why: Close, but slop makers earn money from ads and platform payments. Nobody says the fakes will disappear this year.

mainIdea.s: A famous actor sued a popular video app after fake photos showed him celebrating his 1800th birthday. A judge has now ordered every AI image removed from the internet.
mainIdea.why: The birthday image is just an example of slop. There is no lawsuit and no court order in the article.

tf.s: AI tools can pump out fake content faster than any human could type
tf.why: That speed, plus a cost near zero, is why slop factories treat fakes like a business.

tf.s: Making AI slop is expensive, so only big companies produce it
tf.why: It costs almost nothing to make, and one viral hit can rake in more than a month of honest work.

tf.s: The article says the flood of slop will die down within weeks

tf.why: It costs nothing. Just scroll past strange videos without a second look.

tf.s: Every click on a fake post can mean advertising money for its creator
